**Yes, a cable can limit charging speed.** Charging runs at the lowest of what the charger, the cable, and the device each support. USB-IF notes that a cable doesn't raise the capabilities of the products it connects ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).

**What the ratings mean**
- **60W:** 20V at 3A. USB-IF's own example of a 20V/3A cable carries a 60W logo ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).
- **100W:** 20V at 5A. USB-IF stopped certifying 100W USB-C cables in December 2021, and the spec now defines only 60W and 240W ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)). Older or uncertified cables may still be sold as 100W.
- **240W:** 48V at 5A, called Extended Power Range (EPR). It requires an e-marker chip in the cable, and the spec adds a mandatory 240W mark ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)). The higher voltages (28V for 140W, 36V for 180W, 48V for 240W) come from USB PD 3.1 ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

**How to tell which one you have**
- Look for a 60W or 240W logo on the cable. USB-IF requires one on certified USB-C to USB-C cables.
- With no marking, assume 60W. That is the safe default, and it's enough for phones, tablets, and most thin laptops.
- A 60W cable on a 100W laptop charger will charge, but at 60W at most.

**Whether it matters for you**
- Phones and tablets: it rarely matters, since they draw well under 60W.
- Laptops that draw 65W or more: use a 5A cable (100W or 240W).
- 140W+ laptops, such as 16-inch MacBook Pros: you need a true 240W EPR cable.
